title: The prison opens
hookLine: Bhima wrestles Jarasandha for days; Krishna frees the kings and gives the throne to the fallen king's son
carry: dharma-vijaya: win to set right, not to take

cards: Jarasandha does one thing first. He has his son, Sahadeva, installed as king, so Magadha won't be left without a ruler.

A king who holds other kings in chains still makes sure his own people will have someone on the throne. Then he takes off his crown, binds his hair, and steps out to meet Bhima. No armies, no weapons.
Two men, bare-handed, and a crowd of citizens gathering to watch.

teach.b: They wrestle, the text says, without stopping for food or rest, day and night, for days on end. They grip and throw. They strike with arms and knees.
At last Jarasandha grows tired, and pauses. Krishna speaks a word to Bhima, who takes it as his signal. He lifts Jarasandha high, whirls him around, and brings him down, and the king of Magadha dies.
Here the story could turn into a conquest. It doesn't.
The three go straight to the prison and open it. The captive kings walk out and ask Krishna, what can we do for you? His answer is small: Yudhishthira wants to perform the Rajasuya.
Help him. That's all. Then Jarasandha's son, Sahadeva, comes out with his ministers, bowing low, offering gifts.
Magadha is theirs for the taking, and Krishna gives it back.
He reassures the young man and installs him as king, on his father's throne.

Old Hindu writing on kingship has a name for this kind of win: dharma-vijaya, a righteous victory. There, the righteous conqueror is content once the other side yields; he doesn't grab its land or its family.
Krishna goes further still: he frees the captives, asks only for help with the sacrifice, and leaves the defeated family their home.

teach.h: WIN TO SET RIGHT, NOT TO TAKE.
teach.b: Many teachers read the scene this way: in Hindu eyes, how you win is part of whether you were right. A victory that grabs everything just makes the winner the next Jarasandha.

how: Old Hindu writing on kingship, like the Arthashastra, sets the righteous conqueror, content once the other side yields, against the conqueror who grabs land and wealth; Krishna's handling of Magadha is often told as the picture of a righteous win.

games.q: you're Krishna. Jarasandha is dead, and his son bows before you with gifts. Magadha is yours for the taking. what do you do?
o: make the son king on his father's throne.
leave the kingdom with no king.
games.why: he reassures the young Sahadeva and installs him as king of Magadha. that's dharma-vijaya: the wrong is set right, and the defeated family keeps its home.

practice: There's a Sanskrit prayer many Hindus say: lokah samastah sukhino bhavantu, may all beings everywhere be happy.
Bring to mind someone you came out ahead of, in an argument, a game or a contest, and say it for them, slowly, a few times.
If you don't pray, simply wish them well in your own words, and think of one real thing you could leave them or give back.

wordCard.voice: The Rajasuya. Today, its road opens a prison, and asks the freed kings only for their help, and hands a fallen king's throne to his son.

orig.note: Sanskrit bhīmasena: Bhima's fuller name, the Pandava who wrestles Jarasandha.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma-vijaya, win to set right, not to take. Krishna handed a son his father's throne. Day seven hundred fifty-five, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Jarasandha-vadha Parva (Sahadeva installed; the wrestling; Jarasandha's death; the kings freed; Sahadeva made king of Magadha)
Kautilya, Arthashastra, book 12, ch. 1 (the righteous conqueror, dharmavijayi, content with submission, set against the greedy and the demonic conqueror)
